title: Persian and faith
hookLine: Persian becomes a great language of Islamic poetry: Sa'di, Attar, Hafiz

lines: A BOOK OF POEMS ON THE TABLE.
A NEW PART: PERSIA AND THE TURKS.
cards: In a tea house in Shiraz, a thick book of poems sits on the table. Someone opens it at random, reads the first lines their eye lands on, and the whole table leans in to hear what it says about the week ahead.
The poems are by Hafiz, and some families in Iran still keep this custom: a book of verse treated almost like a friend you can ask for advice. And those poems are in Persian, not Arabic.
A new part of the path begins here: Persia, the Turks and the great empires. It begins with a language. Today: Hafiz.

teach.b: When Islam came to Persia, the language of the Qur'an and of prayer was Arabic, and it stayed that way. Muslims in Iran still pray in Arabic today. But Persian did not disappear.

teach.h: PERSIAN COMES BACK AS A WRITTEN LANGUAGE.
teach.b: It came back as a written language, now in a script borrowed from Arabic and full of Arabic words, and it became a language for poets of the Muslim world. Three names lead the way through the next days.
Attar, who wrote of birds on a long journey. Sa'di of Shiraz, who wrote stories and sayings about how people treat each other.
And Hafiz, also of Shiraz, whose short love poems are read more than one way at once: as songs about human love and wine, and, by some readers, as poems of longing for God.

His pen name is the title Muslims give someone who knows the Qur'an by heart. The Qur'an pays attention to language too. It calls itself, in Pickthall's translation, "a Lecture in Arabic, that ye may understand."

teach.h: THE LANGUAGE OF HIS OWN PEOPLE.
teach.b: Another verse says every messenger was sent with the language of his own people, to make the message clear to them.
For these poets, faith did not need one language only. Prayer stayed in Arabic. Wonder, longing, jokes, advice and grief could come in Persian.
One more detail: Hafiz's collection, as tradition has it, opens on a half-line of Arabic, and then the poem turns into Persian. Two languages, in one breath. The language of poets.

how: Persian poetry by Hafiz, Sa'di, Attar and Rumi is read, recited and memorized in Iran, Afghanistan and beyond, and some families keep the custom of opening Hafiz's collection at random for guidance.

practice: Find one short line by Sa'di, Attar or Hafiz in an English translation, or, with no phone nearby, hold the picture of that tea house table and the open book.
Read the line once for its sense, then again, slower, for its sound and the picture it paints. Is it a poem about people, about God, or both?
